common_name: Golden Harvest Daffodil (Classic Large Golden-Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Golden Harvest is a historic, vigorous large trumpet daffodil dating to the 1930s, still valued for its size and reliable naturalizing.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Golden Harvest is a classic, all-gold trumpet daffodil introduced in the Netherlands in the 1930s, prized for its exceptionally large flowers, broad overlapping perianth petals, and long, flared trumpet held on tall, sturdy stems. Long a mainstay of Dutch bulb production and mass plantings, it remains one of the most dependable and widely available trumpet daffodils for naturalizing in lawns, orchards, and drifts along woodland edges. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Rijnveld's Early Sensation Daffodil (Earliest-Blooming Golden Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Rijnveld's Early Sensation is the earliest trumpet daffodil in general cultivation, often opening in January in mild climates, well ahead of most other daffodils.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in fall. Rijnveld's Early Sensation opens solid golden-yellow trumpet flowers remarkably early, frequently weeks ahead of other trumpet daffodils and sometimes pushing through late snow, which has made it a favorite for the very first color of the bulb season. Its compact stems and dependable, extra-early bloom time make it useful for extending the daffodil display at the start of spring, planted alongside snowdrops and early crocus. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Jumblie is a dwarf triandrus-cyclamineus hybrid daffodil bearing two to three nodding, reflexed flowers per stem, well suited to rock gardens and containers.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Jumblie is a diminutive hybrid daffodil bearing clusters of two to three small, deep golden-yellow flowers per stem with strongly reflexed, swept-back petals and a slightly darker orange-yellow cup, combining the multi-flowered habit of Narcissus triandrus with the wind-blown look of cyclamineus types. Its short stature and early, abundant bloom make it a popular choice for rock gardens, troughs, and the front of borders, where it multiplies readily into dense clumps. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Pueblo Daffodil (Fragrant White Jonquilla Hybrid Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pueblo is a fragrant jonquilla hybrid daffodil bearing multiple small white-and-lemon flowers per stem.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Pueblo bears clusters of two to four small, sweetly fragrant flowers per stem, with a pure white, reflexed perianth surrounding a pale lemon-yellow cup that fades to nearly white as the flower ages, a refined color combination typical of jonquilla hybrids. Its jonquil parentage gives it good heat tolerance and reliable perennializing, and the narrow, rush-like foliage stays tidy after bloom. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize over time.

common_name: Keizerskroon Tulip (Historic Red-and-Yellow Single Early Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Keizerskroon is one of the oldest tulip cultivars still in commerce, dating to 1750, and remains a vigorous, reliable Single Early tulip.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Keizerskroon (Dutch for 'Emperor's Crown') is a historic Single Early tulip dating to 1750, one of the longest-lived tulip cultivars still widely sold, bearing large scarlet-red flowers edged in a bright golden-yellow band along each petal. Its vigor, bold bicolor form, and relatively short, sturdy stems have kept it popular for beds, borders, and forcing for more than two and a half centuries. As with other tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens generally get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than relying on it to perennialize reliably.

common_name: Couleur Cardinal Tulip (Historic Deep Crimson-Purple Triumph Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Couleur Cardinal is a historic Triumph tulip introduced in 1845 and still grown for its rich, velvety color.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Couleur Cardinal is a historic Triumph-type tulip bred by E.H. Krelage and introduced in 1845, bearing deep crimson-scarlet flowers flushed with a purple-bronze sheen on the outer petals that deepens in strong sun, a rich, velvety coloring that has kept it in commerce for more than 175 years. Its sturdy, medium-height stems and reliable, mid-season bloom make it a favorite for beds and cutting. As with other tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens generally get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than relying on it to perennialize reliably.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Purissima, also sold as White Emperor, is a Fosteriana-type tulip prized for blooming very early with unusually large pure white flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Purissima, also widely sold as White Emperor, is a Fosteriana-type tulip that opens creamy-white buds into enormous, pure white, bowl-shaped flowers very early in the tulip season, well ahead of most other cultivars. Its large-scale blooms and sturdy stems make it a striking companion to early Fosteriana types like Red Emperor for a bold two-tone early display. As with other tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens generally get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than relying on it to perennialize reliably.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; as a species tulip, Fusilier bears three to five vivid scarlet flowers per stem and is more likely than hybrid tulips to naturalize.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; species tulips generally tolerate drier, leaner conditions than large hybrid tulips. Fusilier is a multi-flowered selection of Tulipa praestans that sends up several vivid vermilion-scarlet, satiny flowers per stem, opening wide in sun to form a showy cluster rather than the single bloom typical of most hybrid tulips. Its compact stature and reliable, vigorous naturalizing habit make it a popular choice for rock gardens, gravel beds, and mass plantings at the front of a border. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom to support next year's flowering.

common_name: Lilac Wonder Tulip (Fragrant Rosy-Lilac Species Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; as a species tulip native to Crete, Lilac Wonder is more likely than hybrid tulips to naturalize and return for several years.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; species tulips generally tolerate drier, leaner conditions than large hybrid tulips. Lilac Wonder, a selection of the Cretan species Tulipa bakeri, opens fragrant, rosy-lilac flowers with a bright yellow throat, held low on short stems above narrow, grayish-green foliage, closing each evening in the daily rhythm typical of species tulips. Its small scale, fragrance, and strong naturalizing tendency make it a favorite for rock gardens, gravel beds, and the front of a sunny border, where it multiplies readily and is considerably more likely to return in mild-winter Southern gardens than large hybrid tulips. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom to support next year's flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Zomerschoon is one of the oldest tulip cultivars still in cultivation, dating to around 1620, with a naturally 'broken' feathered color pattern.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Zomerschoon ('summer's beauty') is a historic Dutch tulip dating to around 1620, among the oldest tulip cultivars still grown today, bearing an ivory-cream ground irregularly flamed and feathered with soft salmon-apricot, a naturally occurring color-break pattern that once fueled the speculative frenzy of 17th-century tulip mania. Its antique, painterly coloring and sturdy stems make it a prized heirloom for historic gardens and collectors of old Dutch tulip cultivars. As with other tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens generally get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than relying on it to perennialize reliably.

common_name: E.A. Bowles Crocus (Bronze-Feathered Golden Yellow Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; E.A. Bowles is an early, richly colored species crocus named for the English plantsman Edward Augustus Bowles.

directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; good drainage is essential to prevent corm rot during summer dormancy. E.A. Bowles, named for the noted early-20th-century English plantsman and bulb authority Edward Augustus Bowles, bears rich butter-yellow flowers delicately feathered with bronze-purple on the outer petal surfaces, opening early in spring among the first bulbs to bloom and closing on cold or cloudy days to protect the pollen inside. Its warm, antique coloring pairs beautifully with the deeper purples and blues of other early species crocus for a mixed naturalized planting. Allow the narrow, grass-like foliage to die back completely after flowering before mowing over lawn plantings, and it will slowly multiply by cormlets to form larger, denser drifts over the years without needing to be dug and divided.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.

directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Ostara is prized for its rich, deep violet-blue color, among the most saturated blues of any commonly grown hyacinth, opening dense, fragrant spikes that make a bold accent against paler spring bulbs and evergreen foundation plantings. Its deep coloring makes a striking companion to white or pale yellow daffodils and early tulips. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled hyacinth bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since the bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for good flowering in subsequent years without repeat chilling.
